prompt.en: The LUF rises from 4 MHz to 7 MHz while the path MUF stays near 18 MHz. How do plans at 5.3 MHz and 14.2 MHz compare now?

text.en: Both improve equally because a higher lower limit makes every HF band more useful.

feedback.en: Raising the lower edge removes low-frequency choices; it does not improve them.

text.en: 5.3 MHz moves below the usable window; 14.2 MHz stays inside it.

feedback.en: The changed window runs from 7 to 18 MHz. Only the higher example remains inside.

text.en: 14.2 MHz fails first because daytime absorption is always worse at higher HF.

feedback.en: Lower-frequency HF generally suffers more D-region absorption. The forecast still includes 14.2 MHz.

text.en: Both must move exactly to 18 MHz because usable choices equal MUF.

feedback.en: MUF is the upper limit, not a required working frequency. A margin below it is useful.

explanation.en: Recheck both edges of a forecast when conditions change; a fixed MUF does not mean every earlier choice remains useful.

prompt.en: A forecast gives MUF 11.4 MHz and LUF 10.5 MHz. A learner applies 85 % and proposes 9.69 MHz. How should that proposal be judged?

text.en: It is automatically suitable because the multiplication is correct.

feedback.en: The arithmetic is correct, but the result lies below the forecast lower edge.

text.en: It is above the MUF because 85 % raises the starting frequency.

feedback.en: Multiplying by 0.85 lowers the value. The problem is the lower, not upper, boundary.

text.en: It fails the LUF check; the usual planning factor cannot replace checking the whole window.

feedback.en: 9.69 MHz is below 10.5 MHz. A practical factor does not guarantee a usable choice in a narrow window.

text.en: It should be preferred to 10.8 MHz because a lower frequency always suffers less absorption.

feedback.en: Lower HF can suffer greater absorption. The forecast lower limit excludes the proposed 9.69 MHz, while 10.8 MHz lies inside the window.

explanation.en: A useful planning shortcut still has conditions. Check its output against the complete path forecast.

prompt.en: A forecast supports an oblique long-distance path at a frequency above the local vertical critical frequency. Does that alone support a near-vertical regional path at the same frequency?

text.en: Yes, because every path through the same region has the same maximum frequency.

feedback.en: Launch geometry matters. A slant path can return above the vertical limit.

text.en: Yes, if transmitter power is raised until it changes the critical frequency.

feedback.en: Ordinary transmitter power does not set the ionospheric critical frequency.

text.en: Yes, because a high-angle path always needs less bending than a shallow path.

feedback.en: The shallow path needs less bending. A nearly vertical path must use a lower suitable frequency.

text.en: No; the near-vertical path has a different geometry and must meet the vertical-frequency condition.

feedback.en: An oblique path MUF cannot be applied unchanged to NVIS. Check frequency against the relevant near-vertical conditions.

explanation.en: A path-specific forecast is not a blanket approval for every route and launch angle through the region.
